The marímbula is a plucked box instrument of the Caribbean, usually classed with the lamellophones, and it sounds as an idiophone. It is a wooden box with a soundhole in the middle and several metal tongues fixed at one end and tuned to different pitches; the player sits on the box and plucks the tongues downward, at the same time slapping the side like a drum. It mostly provides rhythm and harmonic support and can also play simple melodies. It is found in the Cuban changüí and early son, the Mexican son jarocho, the Dominican merengue típico, Jamaican mento and similar settings.
Marímbula 為加勒比海簧片琴類樂器，常見構造是木製共鳴箱，箱面中央開音孔: The marímbula is a Caribbean lamellophone. It is usually built as a wooden resonating box with a soundhole in the middle of the top; the sounding body is several metal tongues fixed at one end to the box, which give a bass note when plucked. Early instruments used whatever was at hand: discarded wooden crates, elastic wood, bamboo, old saw blades and discarded springs. The source does not state fixed materials for the modern body, tongues and fittings, only that the material of the resonating box and the arrangement of the tongues vary with the design.
Marímbula具非洲根源，19世紀起源於古巴東方省，早期由加勒比非洲奴隸以廢: The marímbula has African roots and originated in Oriente Province, Cuba, in the nineteenth century; early examples were made by enslaved Africans in the Caribbean from discarded crates, springs, bamboo strips and old saw blades, and the player sits on the box, plucking the tongues and slapping the sides. It then spread to Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Mexico and New York City, and to Africa from Liberia to the Congo. In Cuba it is an important bass support in the changüí and old-style son, and the earliest recordings were made in 1925 by Terceto Yoyo and Sexteto Habanero. In Jamaica it is used in mento, and it is currently enjoying a revival among hip hop and mbira players.
Marímbula演奏者通常坐在木箱上方，伸手向下撥動固定在箱體上的金屬簧片發聲: The marímbula player usually sits on top of the wooden box and reaches down to pluck the metal tongues fixed to it, and can slap the side for rhythm at the same time. A beginner first settles the sitting position and the hand position so that the tongues vibrate clearly, keeping to a bass line, and then practises simple melodies and slapping the box in time.
Marímbula的聆聽場合以加勒比海與美洲民間音樂為主。在古巴，它常見於查恩圭: The marímbula is heard mainly in Caribbean and Latin American folk music. In Cuba it is common in the changüí and old-style son; in Mexico it is called the marimbol and used in son jarocho; in the Dominican Republic it is called the marimba and used in merengue típico; in Jamaica it is called the rumba box and used in mento. It has also appeared with guitar, drums, maracas and voices in church, night-club and hotel performances, and in recent years among hip hop and mbira players.

馬林巴琴的音色低沉而溫潤，具有獨特的共鳴感。其音域集中在中低音區，音量適中但具有: The marímbula has a low, warm timbre with a resonance of its own. Its range lies in the middle and lower register, and the volume is moderate but carries well. Because the sound is plucked, each pluck of a metal tongue gives a warm, slightly nasal resonance with a light trace of percussion. The wooden resonating box strengthens the low frequencies and makes the tone fuller. Compared with the guitar, the marímbula is more inward and more rhythmic; compared with traditional percussion it is more tuneful and intimate. These qualities make it an indispensable rhythm instrument in Caribbean folk music, adding a raw and attractive drive underneath.
